extract verb

draw or pull out

also extraction, pull out, draw out, take out (by force), extract a tooth, have a tooth out

classical

Cic. Rosc. Am. 19: tēlum ē corpore (Lewis & Short)
Plin. Ep. 9.33.8

extrahō, extrahere, extrāxī, extractum

verb, third conjugation, transitive · Conjugation on Wiktionary

draw out, pull out, extract

The general word: a weapon from a wound, a net from the water, a person from hiding. Pliny uses dentēs extrahere of drawing teeth with remedies, dentem ēvellere of pulling one by force (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • ēvellō, ēvellere, ēvellī, ēvulsum — pull out, tear out (teeth, nails, weeds)

    verb, third conjugation, transitive · also used · classical · Plin. NH 30.25: dentēs (Lewis & Short); Cic. Sen. 71 · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    To pull out by force; figuratively to root out (a worry, a memory): a favourite of Cicero’s (Lewis & Short).

  • exprimō, exprimere, expressī, expressum — press out, squeeze out (juice, oil)

    verb, third conjugation, transitive · also used · classical · Plin. NH 20.3: sūcum expressō sēminī (Lewis & Short) · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    For extracting a juice or an oil (see squeeze-out). An extract in the chemist’s sense is extractum (M-O s.v. preparation: extract; nineteenth-century pharmacy).

Examples

  • quasi pōma ex arboribus, crūda sī sunt, vix ēvelluntur, sī mātūra et cocta, dēcidunt

    like apples on trees: if they are unripe, they can hardly be pulled off; if ripe and mellow, they fallCic. Sen. 71

  • delphīnum gestātōrem collūsōremque puerōrum in terram quoque extrahī solitum

    the dolphin, the boys’ carrier and playmate, used to be pulled up onto the shore tooPlin. Ep. 9.33.8

See also pull, take out, squeeze out, tooth, pliers, quote.

SourcesLewis & Short: extraho · Lewis & Short: evello · Lewis & Short: exprimo

Cicero and Pliny from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica, loci-plinius); the other passages as Lewis & Short quotes them.

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. preparation: extract.
